guide_description: Three days covering Martha's Vineyard's essential character: the whaling-era captains' town of Edgartown, the Victorian gingerbread camp meeting village of Oak Bluffs, and the remote clay cliffs and tribal lands at the island's western tip. Each day is geographically self-contained and rewards slow exploration on foot or bicycle.

days.cluster_tagline: Federal-era sea captains' mansions, a lighthouse at the harbor mouth, and the island's oldest church
days.neighborhood_description: Martha's Vineyard's county seat and oldest settled town, incorporated in 1671. Edgartown prospered through the 19th-century whaling industry, and the wealth built by that trade survives in a dense concentration of Federal and Greek Revival captains' homes lining North and South Water Streets. The harbor opens onto a narrow channel to Chappaquiddick Island.

morning.notes: The 1939 cast-iron lighthouse sits on a sand spit reached by a short beach walk from the end of North Water Street. Arrive before 10am to have the harborside beach nearly to yourself - the view back toward the white clapboard town with sailboats at anchor is the defining Edgartown image. The Martha's Vineyard Museum operates the lighthouse and sells tower climb tickets seasonally.

afternoon.notes: The museum moved into a converted 1895 Marine Hospital building in 2018, a significant upgrade from the old Cooke House campus. The whaling and maritime galleries are the core, but the exhibit on the island's indigenous Wampanoag history - particularly the Aquinnah Wampanoag - is unusually substantive for a regional maritime museum. The original Fresnel lens from Gay Head Lighthouse is displayed here rather than at the cliff site.

walk_to_next.to: Edgartown Historic District - North Water Street

evening.activity_title: Edgartown Historic District - North and South Water Streets
evening.notes: Walk South Water Street south from the town center - the concentration of intact late Federal and Greek Revival homes is highest in the two-block stretch between Pease's Point Way and Morse Street. The white picket fence on the Vincent House (c. 1672) on Church Street marks the oldest surviving home on the island. Late afternoon light hits the white clapboard facades from the west and turns them gold.

if_time_permits.notes: An 1843 Greek Revival Methodist church built with whaling profits, its six massive wooden columns and 92-foot tower visible from the harbor. The interior has its original box pews and whale-oil lamp fixtures. Now used as a performing arts venue - check the schedule for evening concerts, which are a strong alternative to bar crowds.

walk_from_main_route.from: Edgartown Historic District - North and South Water Streets

if_time_permits.activity_title: Chappaquiddick Island - On Time Ferry crossing
if_time_permits.notes: The On Time Ferry runs 24 hours and holds three cars - but most visitors cross on foot or bicycle. The ferry dock is at the end of Daggett Street, a two-minute walk from the harbor. Chappaquiddick's Mytoi Japanese garden (Trustees of Reservations) is worth the crossing alone if you have a bicycle.

days.cluster_tagline: Camp meeting cottages, a Victorian carousel, and the island's African American heritage corridor
days.neighborhood_description: Originally a Methodist summer camp meeting ground established in 1835, Oak Bluffs grew into a Victorian resort town with a character entirely unlike the rest of the island. The camp meeting core - the Martha's Vineyard Camp Meeting Association grounds, known as the Campground - contains over 300 ornate gingerbread cottages surrounding a cast-iron tabernacle. Oak Bluffs is also the center of the island's long-established African American summer community, rooted in the Highlands neighborhood.

morning.activity_title: Martha's Vineyard Camp Meeting Association Grounds
morning.notes: The Campground is a National Historic Landmark and still a functioning religious community - the lanes between cottages are private property, so stay on the paths and treat it as a neighborhood rather than an attraction. The most photogenic cottages are on Trinity Park and along Siloam Avenue immediately behind the Tabernacle. Morning on weekdays before 10am the lanes are nearly empty.

afternoon.notes: An 1879 cast-iron open-air tabernacle at the center of the Campground - the largest iron tabernacle in the United States. The structure is genuinely remarkable: prefabricated wrought iron arches spanning 130 feet with no interior columns, all seating oriented toward a central pulpit. Community sings and Wednesday night services run through the summer and are open to visitors.

evening.notes: The oldest operating platform carousel in the United States, built in 1876 and moved to Oak Bluffs in 1884. The horses have genuine horsehair manes and glass eyes. The ring game - catching a brass ring from a stationary arm as you ride - is still in operation and earns a free ride. Located at the corner of Circuit and Lake Avenues, one block from the Oak Bluffs harbor ferry dock.

if_time_permits.notes: A seven-acre Victorian seaside park with a bandstand, directly on the water at the southern edge of the Oak Bluffs resort strip. The park faces southeast, which makes it better for morning light than sunset, but the bandstand concerts on summer nights (town band, Wednesday evenings) are a worthwhile reason to linger after dinner.

An 1878 cast-iron lighthouse on the bluff north of Oak Bluffs harbor, painted a distinctive chocolate brown. The grounds are open year-round and the views across Vineyard Haven harbor toward West Chop lighthouse are the best on this side of the island. Accessible by a flat 20-minute walk north along East Chop Drive from the ferry dock.

days.cluster_name: Aquinnah and the Gay Head Cliffs
days.cluster_tagline: Wampanoag tribal lands, ancient clay cliffs, and the island's most remote lighthouse
days.neighborhood_description: The westernmost tip of Martha's Vineyard, belonging to the Aquinnah Wampanoag Tribe, who have inhabited these lands for over 10,000 years. The Gay Head Cliffs - a National Natural Landmark - are layered Cretaceous sediment cliffs rising 150 feet above the Atlantic, striped in red, white, orange, and grey clay. The town of Aquinnah (renamed from Gay Head in 1998) is the most rural part of the island.

morning.notes: Park at the Aquinnah town lot and walk the accessible boardwalk path to the main overlook - the cliffs read best in morning light before the sun moves overhead and flattens the color contrast. Do not descend onto the beach below or touch the clay face; it is tribal land and erosion is a serious ongoing concern. The overlook platform itself gives the full geological cross-section of the Cretaceous layers.

afternoon.notes: The original 1799 lighthouse was replaced by the current brick tower in 1844. In 2015 the entire structure was moved 129 feet back from the eroding cliff edge using a hydraulic roller system - a rare and technically impressive historic preservation operation documented in the visitor materials. The Martha's Vineyard Museum opens the tower for climbs on summer weekends; the view from the top takes in the Elizabeth Islands, Cuttyhunk, and on clear days the Rhode Island coast.

walk_to_next.to: Moshup Trail overlook and Lobsterville Beach

evening.activity_title: Moshup Trail overlook and Lobsterville Beach
evening.notes: The Moshup Trail road runs along the south shore bluff east of the cliffs toward the Lobsterville Beach area - the western-facing shore that catches the full Atlantic sunset with no obstructions. Parking is limited and metered in summer; arriving by bicycle from Oak Bluffs along the state road bike path (roughly 10 miles each way) is the preferred approach for travelers who rent bikes in Edgartown or Oak Bluffs. The trail is named for the Wampanoag culture hero Moshup, whose legends are tied to the cliff geology.

if_time_permits.notes: A small tribal cultural center near the Gay Head Cliffs parking area operated by the Aquinnah Wampanoag Tribe. Exhibits cover the tribe's 10,000-year presence on the island, the 1987 federal recognition process, and the ongoing relationship between the tribe and the cliff landscape. Worth visiting before the cliffs rather than after, to give context to what you're seeing.
